e-4348.knowledge_point: Calculating the Scalar Triple Product Using a Determinant
e-4348.worked_solution:
Remember that the scalar triple product $\mathbf{a} \cdot (\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{c})$ is just the determinant of the matrix whose rows are given by $\mathbf{a},$ $\mathbf{b},$ and $\mathbf{c}.$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a\cdot (b\times c) & =|\begin{aligned}4 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}|+(-1)\cdot |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =4\cdot (2\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1))-2\cdot (0\cdot 2-1\cdot (-1))+(-1)\cdot (0\cdot (-1)-2\cdot (-1)) \\  & =20-2-2 \\  & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

e-4349.knowledge_point: Calculating Scalar Triple Products Using Its Properties
e-4349.worked_solution:
First, we factor out the constants and get

$$
\begin{aligned}2a\cdot (b\times 3c) & =5 \\ 2\cdot [a\cdot (b\times 3c)] & =5 \\ 2\cdot 3\cdot [a\cdot (b\times c)] & =5 \\ a\cdot (b\times c) & =\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot (b\times a) & =-\frac{5}{6},\end{aligned}
$$

and again we swap $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}c\cdot (a\times b) & =\frac{5}{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
